claim: Recent advances in tissue processing, labeling, and fluorescence microscopy are providing unprecedented views of the structure of cells and tissues at sub-diffraction resolutions and near single molecule sensitivity.
source: Recent advances in tissue processing, labeling, and fluorescence microscopy are providing unprecedented views of the structure of cells and tissues at sub-diffraction resolutions and near single molecule sensitivity, driving discoveries in diverse fields of biology, including neuroscience.
evidence: This is a general statement about recent advances in the field, supported by the context of the manuscript and citations throughout the introduction.

claim: Biological tissue is organized over scales of nanometers to centimeters.
source: Biological tissue is organized over scales of nanometers to centimeters.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in biology, representing general scientific knowledge.

claim: Standard microscope objectives with high resolutions have limited working distances (<1 mm) and fields of view (<1 mm).
source: However, standard microscope objectives with high resolutions have limited working distances (<1 mm) and fields of view (<1 mm).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Zhang and Gross, 2019b and general knowledge about microscope objectives.

claim: Imaging large tissue volumes at high resolutions requires physical sectioning and extensive tiling.
source: Imaging large tissue volumes at high resolutions therefore requires physical sectioning and extensive tiling.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the limitations of standard microscope objectives and is supported by common practice in the field.

claim: Physical sectioning distorts the imaged tissue.
source: Physical sectioning distorts the imaged tissue, and focal planes have optical distortions at the edges of the field of view (Zhang and Gross, 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Zhang and Gross, 2019b.

claim: Focal planes have optical distortions at the edges of the field of view.
source: Physical sectioning distorts the imaged tissue, and focal planes have optical distortions at the edges of the field of view (Zhang and Gross, 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Zhang and Gross, 2019b.

claim: Light aberration and scattering limit high-resolution microscopy in tissue to depths of hundreds of micrometers.
source: Because light aberration and scattering limit high-resolution microscopy in tissue, including two-photon microscopy, to depths of hundreds of micrometers, sectioning and tiling have traditionally been viewed as necessary to image large specimens (Portera-Cailliau et al., 2005; Tsai et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2014; Economo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Portera-Cailliau et al., 2005; Tsai et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2014; Economo et al., 2016).

claim: Advances in histological methods, including clearing and expansion, now promise diffraction-limited imaging deep in tissue.
source: However, advances in histological methods, including clearing (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Spalteholz, 1914; Dodt et al., 2007; Tsai et al., 2009; Hama et al., 2011; Becker et al., 2012; Ertürk et al., 2012; Chung and Deisseroth, 2013; Ke et al., 2013; Susaki et al., 2014; Tainaka et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2014; Renier et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2015; Costantini et al., 2015; Chi et al., 2018) and expansion for microscopy (ExM; Chen et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Chozinski et al., 2016; Ku et al., 2016), now promise diffraction-limited imaging deep in tissue.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to clearing and expansion microscopy methods.

claim: Expansion up to 20× has been demonstrated.
source: Expansion up to 20×has been demonstrated (Chang et al., 2017), which provides access to molecular spatial scales (10's of nm), approaching those of cryo electron microscopy (a few nm; Cheng et al., 2015; Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016; Nogales and Scheres, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Chang et al., 2017.

claim: 20× expansion provides access to molecular spatial scales (10's of nm), approaching those of cryo electron microscopy (a few nm).
source: Expansion up to 20×has been demonstrated (Chang et al., 2017), which provides access to molecular spatial scales (10's of nm), approaching those of cryo electron microscopy (a few nm; Cheng et al., 2015; Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016; Nogales and Scheres, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cryo electron microscopy (Cheng et al., 2015; Fernandez-Leiro and Scheres, 2016; Nogales and Scheres, 2015) and is a logical inference from the expansion factor.

claim: ExA-SPIM combines a new microscope and methods for tissue clearing and expansion.
source: We combine a new microscope and methods for tissue clearing and expansion, which we jointly refer to as Expansion-Assisted Selective Plane Illumination Microscopy (ExA-SPIM).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: Expansion lattice light-sheet microscopy is limited to small tissue volumes << 1 mm3.
source: Unlike expansion lattice light-sheet microscopy (Gao et al., 2023), which is limited to small tissue volumes << 1 mm3, ExA-SPIM works with expansion of large centimeter-scale tissue volumes, such as the mouse brain.
evidence: This is supported by the citation Gao et al., 2023.

claim: ExA-SPIM works with expansion of large centimeter-scale tissue volumes, such as the mouse brain.
source: Unlike expansion lattice light-sheet microscopy (Gao et al., 2023), which is limited to small tissue volumes << 1 mm3, ExA-SPIM works with expansion of large centimeter-scale tissue volumes, such as the mouse brain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data presented in the manuscript, including imaging of entire mouse brains.

claim: ExA-SPIM has a field of view ~100 × larger (13.3 mm diameter) compared to objectives typically used for biological microscopy.
source: Leveraging optics and detectors developed for the electronics metrology industry, ExA-SPIM has a field of view ~100 × larger (13.3 mm diameter) and a working distance ~10 × larger (35 mm) compared to objectives typically used for biological microscopy, while retaining a relatively high numerical aperture (NA)=0.305.
evidence: This is supported by the specifications of the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: ExA-SPIM has a working distance ~10 × larger (35 mm) compared to objectives typically used for biological microscopy.
source: Leveraging optics and detectors developed for the electronics metrology industry, ExA-SPIM has a field of view ~100 × larger (13.3 mm diameter) and a working distance ~10 × larger (35 mm) compared to objectives typically used for biological microscopy, while retaining a relatively high numerical aperture (NA)=0.305.
evidence: This is supported by the specifications of the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: ExA-SPIM retains a relatively high numerical aperture (NA)=0.305.
source: Leveraging optics and detectors developed for the electronics metrology industry, ExA-SPIM has a field of view ~100 × larger (13.3 mm diameter) and a working distance ~10 × larger (35 mm) compared to objectives typically used for biological microscopy, while retaining a relatively high numerical aperture (NA)=0.305.
evidence: This is supported by the specifications of the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: When combined with 3×expansion, the ExA-SPIM system achieves an effective resolution of ~0.5 µm laterally, and ~1 µm axially.
source: When combined with 3×expansion, the system achieves an effective resolution of ~0.5 µm laterally, and ~1 µm axially, at imaging speeds of up to 946 megavoxels/s.
evidence: This is supported by the specifications and measurements of the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: ExA-SPIM achieves imaging speeds of up to 946 megavoxels/s.
source: When combined with 3×expansion, the system achieves an effective resolution of ~0.5 µm laterally, and ~1 µm axially, at imaging speeds of up to 946 megavoxels/s.
evidence: This is supported by the specifications of the ExA-SPIM system described in the manuscript.

claim: Imaging with diffraction-limited resolution throughout centimeter-scale specimens requires tissue samples with small index of refraction variations.
source: Imaging with diffraction-limited resolution throughout centimeter-scale specimens requires tissue samples with small index of refraction variations (Weiss et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Weiss et al., 2021.

claim: Axonal arbors of individual neurons are complex, branched structures that transmit electrical impulses over distances of centimeters.
source: Axonal arbors of individual neurons are complex, branched structures that transmit electrical impulses over distances of centimeters, yet axons can be thinner than 100 nm (Economo et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Economo et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2019) and is general knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: Axons can be thinner than 100 nm.
source: Axonal arbors of individual neurons are complex, branched structures that transmit electrical impulses over distances of centimeters, yet axons can be thinner than 100 nm (Economo et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Economo et al., 2016; Winnubst et al., 2019).

claim: Tracing the axonal arbors of single neurons is critical to define how signals are routed within the brain.
source: Tracing the axonal arbors of single neurons is critical to define how signals are routed within the brain and is also necessary for classifying diverse neuron types into distinct types (Economo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Winnubst et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Economo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Winnubst et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).

claim: Tracing the axonal arbors of single neurons is necessary for classifying diverse neuron types into distinct types.
source: Tracing the axonal arbors of single neurons is critical to define how signals are routed within the brain and is also necessary for classifying diverse neuron types into distinct types (Economo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Winnubst et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Economo et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2021; Winnubst et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).

claim: Large-scale projects based on single-cell transcriptomics in the mouse and human brain have revealed a great diversity of neuron types.
source: Large-scale projects based on single-cell transcriptomics in the mouse and human brain have revealed a great diversity of neuron types (Hodge et al., 2019; Tasic et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Hodge et al., 2019; Tasic et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2023).

claim: The throughput of neuronal reconstructions has remained too low for single neuron reconstructions on a comparable scale, even in mice.
source: However, the throughput of neuronal reconstructions has remained too low for single neuron reconstructions on a comparable scale, even in mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of the field and the need for improved methods.

claim: Throughput is limited in part by speed and image quality of existing microscopy methods.
source: Throughput is limited in part by speed and image quality of existing microscopy methods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of existing methods and the need for improved microscopy.

claim: ExA-SPIM provides high-resolution fluorescence microscopy over teravoxel image volumes with minimal distortions.
source: We demonstrate that ExA-SPIM provides high-resolution fluorescence microscopy over teravoxel image volumes with minimal distortions, and thereby enables brain-wide imaging with high contrast, resolution, and speed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ExA-SPIM enables brain-wide imaging with high contrast, resolution, and speed.
source: We demonstrate that ExA-SPIM provides high-resolution fluorescence microscopy over teravoxel image volumes with minimal distortions, and thereby enables brain-wide imaging with high contrast, resolution, and speed.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data presented in the manuscript, including imaging of entire mouse brains.

claim: The etendue (G) is proportional to the number of resolution elements of an optical system.
source: The trade-off between resolution and field of view is related to the etendue (G), which is proportional to the number of resolution elements of an optical system.
evidence: This is a definition from optics and is general knowledge in the field.

claim: The etendue is a quadratic function of the lens field of view (FOV) and numerical aperture (NA).
source: The etendue is a quadratic function of the lens field of view (FOV) and numerical aperture (NA).
evidence: This is supported by the equation provided in the manuscript: G = (π/4)(FOV × NA)^2.

claim: For a given NA, the required lens diameter increases proportionally with the required working distance (WD).
source: Similarly, for a given NA, the required lens diameter increases proportionally with the required working distance (WD).
evidence: This is a principle of optical design and is general knowledge in the field.

claim: 90% of commercially available objectives for biological microscopy have G<1 mm2.
source: 90% of commercially available objectives for biological microscopy have G<1 mm2 (Zhang and Gross, 2019a), and the vast majority of commercially available lenses have lens diameters < 2 cm.
evidence: This is supported by the citation Zhang and Gross, 2019a.

claim: The vast majority of commercially available lenses have lens diameters < 2 cm.
source: 90% of commercially available objectives for biological microscopy have G<1 mm2 (Zhang and Gross, 2019a), and the vast majority of commercially available lenses have lens diameters < 2 cm.
evidence: This is an inference based on the general state of commercially available lenses.

claim: The 'Mesolens' provides an etendue of G=6.25 mm2, with FOV = 6 mm, NA = 0.47, and WD = 3 mm.
source: The 'Mesolens' provides an etendue of G=6.25 mm2, with FOV = 6 mm, NA = 0.47, and WD = 3 mm (McConnell et al., 2016), but difficulties with manufacturing have limited adoption (McConnell, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the citations (McConnell et al., 2016; McConnell, 2020).

claim: Difficulties with manufacturing have limited adoption of the Mesolens.
source: The 'Mesolens' provides an etendue of G=6.25 mm2, with FOV = 6 mm, NA = 0.47, and WD = 3 mm (McConnell et al., 2016), but difficulties with manufacturing have limited adoption (McConnell, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the citation McConnell, 2020.

claim: An objective with an etendue of G=7.07 mm2, FOV = 5 mm, NA = 0.6, and WD = 2.7 mm has been developed for two-photon microscopy in vivo.
source: An objective with an etendue of G=7.07 mm2, FOV = 5 mm, NA = 0.6, and WD = 2.7 mm has been developed for two-photon microscopy in vivo (Sofroniew et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Sofroniew et al., 2016.

claim: The objective developed by Sofroniew et al., 2016 is customized for infrared illumination and exhibits significant field curvature.
source: However, this lens is customized for infrared illumination and exhibits significant field curvature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the description of the lens and its intended use.

claim: A custom lens with a large etendue of G=18.86 mm2, FOV = 14 mm, NA = 0.35, and WD = 19 mm has been developed for the RUSH microscope.
source: A custom lens with a large etendue of G=18.86 mm2, FOV = 14 mm, NA = 0.35, and WD = 19 mm has been developed for the real-time ultra-large-scale high-resolution (RUSH) microscope (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the citation Fan et al., 2019.

claim: The RUSH lens is not commercially available and not designed for immersion.
source: Despite the large etendue, the lens is not commercially available and not designed for immersion, which is critical for imaging cleared or expanded tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the description of the lens and its limitations.

claim: High-resolution, high-speed imaging is widely used within the machine vision and metrology industry.
source: High-resolution, high-speed imaging is widely used within the machine vision and metrology industry, where optical microscopes are used to map defects in semiconductors and other electronic devices.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the machine vision and metrology industry.

claim: As the physical size of electronic components has become smaller, lenses for the metrology industry have been designed with increasing NA, accessing biologically relevant resolutions (<1 µm).
source: As the physical size of electronic components (e.g. pixels on flat panel displays) has become smaller, lenses for this domain have been designed with increasing NA, accessing biologically relevant resolutions (<1 µm).
evidence: This is an inference based on the development of lenses for the metrology industry.

claim: For a given NA, metrology lenses have remarkably large fields of view (and thus high etendues), low-field curvature, minimal distortion, and chromatic correction throughout the visible wavelengths.
source: For a given NA, these lenses have remarkably large fields of view (and thus high etendues), low-field curvature, minimal distortion, and chromatic correction throughout the visible wavelengths.
evidence: This is a description of the properties of metrology lenses.

claim: Metrology optics and cameras are readily available, are manufactured in large quantities, and are cost effective.
source: Despite their superb specifications, both the lenses and camera sensors are readily available, are manufactured in large quantities, and are cost effective.
evidence: This is a statement about the availability and cost of metrology optics and cameras.

claim: The detection path of the ExA-SPIM system uses a lens with 5.0×magnification, with diffraction-limited imaging at NA = 0.305, and a 16.8 mm field of view (G=19.65 mm2).
source: The detection path of the system uses a lens with 5.0×magnification, with diffraction-limited imaging at NA = 0.305, and a 16.8 mm field of view (G=19.65 mm2) (VEO_JM DIAMOND 5.0×/F1.3, Schneider-Kreuznach, Germany) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: A 35-mm-thick glass beam splitter is replaced with an optically equivalent thickness of liquid media in the ExA-SPIM system.
source: A 35-mm-thick glass beam splitter, normally used for co-axial illumination, is replaced with an optically equivalent thickness of liquid media.
evidence: This is a description of the ExA-SPIM system design.

claim: Replacing the beam splitter with liquid media enables spherical aberration-free imaging through 35–40 mm of liquid media.
source: This enables spherical aberration-free imaging through 35–40 mm of liquid media (tunable for refractive indices between 1.33 and 1.56), including expanded hydrogels and cleared tissues.
evidence: This is a description of the ExA-SPIM system design and its capabilities.

claim: The lens is paired with a large-format CMOS sensor (VP-151MX, Vieworks Korea), based on the Sony IMX411 sensor, with a single-sided rolling shutter, 151 megapixels, 14192 (H)×10,640 (V), and a pitch of 3.76 µm.
source: The lens is paired with a large-format CMOS sensor (VP-151MX, Vieworks Korea), based on the Sony IMX411 sensor, with a single-sided rolling shutter, 151 megapixels, 14192 (H)×10,640 (V), and a pitch of 3.76 µm.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: The camera captures a field of view of 10.6×8.0 mm (13.3 mm diagonal), capable of covering an entire 3×expanded mouse brain in only 15 tiles.
source: The camera captures a field of view of 10.6×8.0 mm (13.3 mm diagonal), capable of covering an entire 3×expanded mouse brain in only 15 tiles (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system and is demonstrated in Figure 2b.

claim: A conventional SPIM system would require 400+tiles to image an entire cleared brain at equivalent resolutions.
source: A conventional SPIM system would require 400+tiles to image an entire cleared brain at equivalent resolutions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to conventional SPIM systems and is illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ExA-SPIM system synchronizes an axially-swept light sheet with the rolling shutter of the Sony IMX411 sensor.
source: To improve axial resolution, our system synchronizes an axially-swept light sheet with the rolling shutter of the Sony IMX411 sensor (Dean et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the ExA-SPIM system design, supported by the citation Dean et al., 2015.

claim: The CMOS sensor parallelizes readout across 14192 pixels per row, thereby achieving equivalent or greater pixel rates than typical scientific CMOS (sCMOS) sensors.
source: The CMOS sensor parallelizes readout across 14192 pixels per row, thereby achieving equivalent or greater pixel rates than typical scientific CMOS (sCMOS) sensors, even with an increased time per line and a relatively low frame rate (<6.4 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the CMOS sensor capabilities.

claim: The ExA-SPIM microscope operates at a higher imaging speed with comparable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to sCMOS-based systems.
source: As a result, the ExA-SPIM microscope operates at a higher imaging speed with comparable signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to sCMOS-based systems (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2e.

claim: The low frame rate of the sensor facilitates accurate axially swept imaging using generic scanning hardware at an imaging speed of 946 megavoxels/sec.
source: The low frame rate of the sensor facilitates accurate axially swept imaging using generic scanning hardware at an imaging speed of 946 megavoxels/sec.
evidence: This is a description of the ExA-SPIM system capabilities.

claim: The excitation lens (1–290419, Navitar) is infinity-corrected and provides diffraction-limited resolution at NA = 0.133 over a 16 mm field of view.
source: The excitation lens (1–290419, Navitar) is infinity-corrected (to enable axially swept excitation) and provides diffraction-limited resolution at NA = 0.133 over a 16 mm field of view.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: When fitted with a custom dipping cap, the excitation lens provides a working distance of 53 mm in water.
source: When fitted with a custom dipping cap, the excitation lens provides a working distance of 53 mm in water.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: The beam shaping in the excitation path is configured to deliver a light sheet with NA = 0.10 and width of 12.5 mm (full-width half-maximum).
source: The beam shaping in the excitation path is configured to deliver a light sheet with NA = 0.10 and width of 12.5 mm (full-width half-maximum).
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: The ExA-SPIM system uses high excitation laser powers (1000+mW).
source: Due to the large light-sheet, the ExA-SPIM system uses high excitation laser powers (1000+mW; Figure 2—figure supplement 5), resulting in light intensities typically used in SPIM microscopy.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system and is illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The high excitation laser powers result in light intensities typically used in SPIM microscopy.
source: Due to the large light-sheet, the ExA-SPIM system uses high excitation laser powers (1000+mW; Figure 2—figure supplement 5), resulting in light intensities typically used in SPIM microscopy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the large light sheet and high laser powers.

claim: Photobleaching is not detrimental at the imaging conditions used by ExA-SPIM.
source: Photobleaching is not detrimental at these imaging conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The ExA-SPIM is capable of imaging a 200×52 × 35 mm3 volume, with ~1.5 µm lateral and ~3 µm axial native optical resolution, and minimal field curvature and distortion.
source: Based on these lenses, and the travel limits of a mechanical motorized stage, the ExA-SPIM is capable of imaging a 200×52 × 35 mm3 volume, with ~1.5 µm lateral and ~3 µm axial native optical resolution, and minimal field curvature quantified using the methodology described in Vladimirov et al., 2024 and distortion (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system and is demonstrated in Figure 2c-d.

claim: With 3×tissue expansion, the ExA-SPIM system can image a native tissue volume of 67×17 × 12 mm3 with an effective optical resolution of ~0.5 µm laterally and ~1 µm axially.
source: With 3×tissue expansion, the system can image a native tissue volume of 67×17 × 12 mm3 with an effective optical resolution of ~0.5 µm laterally and ~1 µm axially.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system with tissue expansion.

claim: The ExA-SPIM system can image >100 teravoxels without the need for physical sectioning and with minimal tiling.
source: This amounts to >100 teravoxels, which can be captured without the need for physical sectioning and with minimal tiling.
evidence: This is a specification of the ExA-SPIM system capabilities.

claim: The large field of view of the ExA-SPIM system can permit imaging cleared tissues, such as mouse brains, in a single tile.
source: The large field of view of the ExA-SPIM system can also permit imaging cleared tissues, such as mouse brains, in a single tile (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The large-scale and high-speed imaging made possible by the ExA-SPIM system required new software for controlling the microscope.
source: The large-scale and high-speed imaging made possible by the ExA-SPIM system required new software for controlling the microscope, as well as downstream computational pipelines for compressing and handling the resulting datasets (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a description of the software development for the ExA-SPIM system.

claim: Custom acquisition software was developed capable of interfacing with the VP-151MX camera driver, which streams imaging data directly to next-generation file formats.
source: We developed custom acquisition software capable of interfacing with the VP-151MX camera driver (https://github.com/acquire-project), which streams imaging data directly to next-generation file formats (Beati et al., 2020; Clack et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the software development for the ExA-SPIM system, supported by citations (Beati et al., 2020; Clack et al., 2023; Moore et al., 2021).

claim: The imaging pipeline enables a throughput to cloud storage of >100 TB per day, using commodity hardware.
source: Using a combination of high-speed networking, fast on-premises storage, and real-time compression, our current imaging pipeline enables a throughput to cloud storage of >100 TB per day, using commodity hardware.
evidence: This is a specification of the imaging pipeline capabilities.

claim: Tissue expansion for microscopy (ExM) enables imaging optically transparent specimens at effective resolutions well below the diffraction limit of light microscopes.
source: Tissue expansion for microscopy (ExM) enables imaging optically transparent specimens at effective resolutions well below the diffraction limit of light microscopes (Chang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg and Chen, 2019; Figure 2—figure supplement 10).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Chang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2015; Tillberg and Chen, 2019) and is illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 10.

claim: ExM can produce optically clear specimens with low fluorescence background.
source: Moreover, ExM can produce optically clear specimens with low fluorescence background.
evidence: This is a known property of ExM methods.

claim: Multiple ExM variations have emerged, driven by specific biological questions.
source: Multiple ExM variations have emerged, driven by specific biological questions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the development of ExM methods.

claim: Most ExM protocols have been developed for specimens that are at most 100 micrometers thick.
source: Most of these protocols have been developed for specimens that are at most 100 micrometers thick.
evidence: This is an inference based on the typical applications of ExM methods.

claim: ExM methods were developed for centimeter-scale tissue samples, including entire mouse brains.
source: We developed ExM methods for centimeter-scale tissue samples, including entire mouse brains.
evidence: This is a description of the methods developed in the manuscript.

claim: A key requirement for ExA-SPIM is optical clearing so that the entire volume can be imaged with diffraction-limited resolution without sectioning.
source: A key requirement for ExA-SPIM is optical clearing so that the entire volume can be imaged with diffraction-limited resolution without sectioning.
evidence: This is a description of the requirements for ExA-SPIM.

claim: Index of refraction inhomogeneities in heavily myelinated fiber tracts pose particular challenges for optical clearing.
source: Index of refraction inhomogeneities in heavily myelinated fiber tracts pose particular challenges.
evidence: This is a known challenge in optical clearing of brain tissue.

claim: Clearing was achieved by stringent dehydration and delipidation prior to gelation and expansion.
source: Clearing was achieved by stringent dehydration and delipidation prior to gelation and expansion.
evidence: This is a description of the clearing protocol developed in the manuscript.

claim: Dehydration using THF was followed by two sequential delipidation steps.
source: Dehydration using THF was followed by two sequential delipidation steps.
evidence: This is a description of the clearing protocol developed in the manuscript.

claim: DISCO type clearing followed by aqueous delipidation rendered the samples extremely transparent.
source: First DISCO type clearing Chi et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2014 followed by aqueous delipidation (Chen and Svoboda, 2020c, dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.zndf5a6) rendered the samples extremely transparent (Figure 3a; Ouellette et al., 2023, dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.n92ldpwjxl5b/v1).
evidence: This is a description of the clearing protocol developed in the manuscript, supported by citations (Chi et al., 2018; Renier et al., 2014; Chen and Svoboda, 2020c; Ouellette et al., 2023) and demonstrated in Figure 3a.

claim: Delipidation facilitates immunolabeling brain samples prior to gelation and expansion.
source: In addition to clearing specimens, delipidation facilitates immunolabeling brain samples prior to gelation and expansion (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the benefits of delipidation and is demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Signal amplification facilitates high contrast imaging of small structures, especially since the increase in volume upon expansion dilutes the concentration of the fluorophore.
source: Signal amplification facilitates high contrast imaging of small structures, especially since the increase in volume upon expansion dilutes the concentration of the fluorophore.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of signal amplification in expansion microscopy.

claim: VA-044 was used as the initiator for gelation, instead of the more commonly used APS/TEMED.
source: For gelation, we used VA-044 as the initiator, instead of the more commonly used APS/TEMED (Tillberg and Chen, 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the gelation protocol developed in the manuscript, with a citation to Tillberg and Chen, 2019.

claim: VA-044 initiates free radicals at a temperature-dependent rate.
source: VA-044 initiates free radicals at a temperature-dependent rate.
evidence: This is a known property of VA-044.

claim: At low temperatures (4 °C), the gelling reagents are allowed to diffuse to the center of thick samples, followed by higher temperatures (37 °C) to trigger uniform polymerization.
source: At low temperatures (4 °C), the gelling reagents are allowed to diffuse to the center of thick samples, followed by higher temperatures (37 °C) to trigger uniform polymerization.
evidence: This is a description of the gelation protocol developed in the manuscript.

claim: The protocol provides nearly isotropic expansion of the whole sample (including internal brain structures).
source: Our protocol provides nearly isotropic expansion of the whole sample (including internal brain structures).
evidence: This is a description of the properties of the expansion protocol developed in the manuscript.

claim: The protocol has been successfully used for other large specimens, such as a 1 cm×1 cm×1.5 cm piece of macaque motor cortex, as well as a 1 cm×1 cm×0.01 cm section of human visual cortex.
source: Although developed for the mouse brain, we have successfully used this protocol for other large specimens, such as a 1 cm×1 cm×1.5 cm piece of macaque motor cortex, as well as a 1 cm×1 cm×0.01 cm section of human visual cortex (Ouellette et al., 2023, dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.n92ldpwjxl5b/v1).
